text: Hello, everyone. Thank you for the opportunity.
I am Md Abrarul Faisal.
I recently completed my MSc in Oceanography, from Shahjalal
University of Science and Technology, Bangladesh.
Today, I will present my research
on evaluating four machine learning algorithms, using Google Earth Engine
for analyzing LULC dynamics
of Sundarban Island, Bangladesh.
Land use land cover is important for understanding
environmental changes, natural resource management, and coastal
development.
In this study, I used remote sensing and Google Earth Engine
to analyze LULC changes and compared four machine
learning algorithms
... which are CART, SVM, Random Forest, and Gradient Tree Boost.
Bangladesh is a delta country, and the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna
river system
brings a huge amount of sediment to the coast.
This creates continuous erosion and accretion.
At the same time, population growth, infrastructure, climate
change, and aquaculture are putting heavy pressure on coastal areas.
Sandwip Island is particularly dynamic, but it remains
relatively understudied.
Therefore, my objectives were to analyze its
shoreline changes, also detect LULC changes using machine
learning algorithms, and compare their classification
accuracy.
This is the study area map,
and I used Landsat and Sentinel-2 satellite
imagery for the analysis,
also covering long-term changes in both
shoreline and land cover.
The methodology had two main parts.
For shoreline analysis, I used satellite images from
I extracted shoreline in ArcGIS and used DSAS to
calculate EPR, NSM, and LRR.
And for LULC analysis,
I used images from 2000 to 2025.
After preprocessing and collecting training samples, I classified the
images using CART, SVM, Random Forest, and GBT.
Finally, I performed accuracy assessment and change detection.
For onshore shoreline,
the EPR ranged from
to +203.3 meters per year.
This indicates that different parts of Sandwip experience
both erosion and accretion.
For the offshore shoreline, the EPR
ranged from -245.2 to
+572.9 meters per year.
This again shows that Sandwip has a highly dynamic
shoreline, with
both erosion and accretion occurring around the island.
Here, I compared the LULC maps produced by the four
algorithms.
CART showed more mixed pixels, while
SVM showed some overgeneralizations.
Random Forest produced the cleanest and most reliable-looking
map,
while GBT performed relatively close to Random Forest.
The performance varied between individual LULC classes.
SVM performed best for built-up areas, while Random Forest performed
particularly well for sandy areas and
several other classes.
So the performance depended on the specific land cover
classes.
To determine the best overall classifier,
I used 140 ground truth points, with
20 points for each of the seven classes.

Now, looking at the LULC changes from 2000 and
Vegetation and cropland dominated much of the island's interior.
Sandy and barren land were mainly concentrated in the northern
and southeastern parts.
And over time, built-up area increased, vegetation
expanded, and mangrove area also increased.
Sandy and barren areas showed change over time,
while
water bodies remained relatively stable.
Overall, the land cover pattern becomes increasingly
influenced by both vegetation growth and human development.
By the
end of the study period, vegetation and cropland still
dominated the island's interior.
Built-up area
continued to expand, sandy area generally decreased,
and
mangrove patches become larger and more connected.
Water bodies showed no major changes.
For change detection, Random Forest
results clearly showed these changes.
Built-up area increased from approximately 18.1
square kilometer in 2000 to 60
square kilometer in 2024.
Barren land decreased from about 101.1
square kilometer to 23.5 square kilometer.
Which is significant, and
mangrove increased from approximately 17.7 to
27.4 square kilometers.
This confirms major changes in the island's land cover
composition.
To conclude, Shonib Island is experiencing significant
shoreline and LULC changes.
The
island experienced
accretion mainly in the east and
southeast, while
erosion continued in the west.
Among the four machine learning algorithms, random forest
performed best with 93.57%
overall accuracy.
The LULC results also showed expansion of
vegetation, agriculture, mangrove, and built-up areas.
In future, integrating sediment modeling, hydrodynamics, and
environmental parameters could improve shoreline and LULC assessment.
